newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq cracks down on smuggling, banned goods.
newsitem.headline: Iraq cracks down on smuggling, banned goods.

text.p: Iraq, its economy hit hard by U.N. trade sanctions imposed after it invaded Kuwait in 1990, is cracking down on smuggling and traffic in banned goods.

The Revolutionary Command Council (RCC) said in a decree signed by President Saddam Hussein and published in newspapers on Sunday that authorities could seize "property bound for smuggling and property banned from circulation in the local market".
It is the third time in four years that Iraq has attempted such a crackdown.
Banned foreign goods include toys, computers, beer and spirits, chicken, cheese, candy, cigarettes, perfume, videos, watches, vacuum cleaners, clothes, shoes, radios and cassette recorders.
Traders had been allowed to deal in two kinds of imported goods -- basic foods, exempt from customs duties, and a heavily taxed list of permitted spare parts and agricultural tools.
As time passed, authorities relaxed controls and various foreign goods returned to the market.

Since the government lifted an embargo in northern Iraq after the recent victory by a Baghdad-backed Kurdish group over rival Kurds, markets have been flooded with foreign goods. The fighting halted last week under a U.S.-sponsored ceasefire.
Shops in smart areas in Baghdad are loaded with foreign electrical goods, sweets, tinned foods and beverages -- real luxuries for many Iraqis.
The battered dinar currency, now trading at about 1,800 to the U.S. dollar, has made Iraq a haven for smugglers.
Under the decree, committees will be formed in each province to receive items that will be confiscated and handed over to ministries. The RCC also offered rewards to informers.
Imported goods are beyond the reach of most Iraqis. One kg (2.2 lb) of imported cheese sells for 6,000 dinars, more than the average civil servant's salary.
Most imports enter from Jordan, Turkey or the Kurdish rebel-held areas in the north.
The RCC also imposed a further fee of 500 dinars on Iraqis travelling abroad, adding to the 400,000-dinar fee already in force.
